:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\nabla f(x,y,z)  = \mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = yz\,\mathbf{i} + (xz + 4z^2)\,\mathbf{j} + (xy+8yz)\,\mathbf{k}.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} \, \mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} \, \mathbf{j} + \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} \, \mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)  = \mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}} = yz, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2, \qquad \dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz.
$$

First, we integrate $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{x}}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int yz\,\text{d}x \\  & =xyz+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + \dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}.
$$

Taking $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{y}} = xz + 4z^2$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xz+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =xz+4{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =4{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\dfrac{\partial{g}}{\partial{y}}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 4{z}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z) = 4yz^2 + h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x, y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy + 8yz + h'(z).
$$

Taking $\dfrac{\partial{f}}{\partial{z}} = xy+8yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy+8yz & =xy+8yz+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z) = xyz + 4yz^2 + C.
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: f(x, y, z) = x^{2}yz + yz^{2} + C
f(x, y, z) = x^{2}y + yz + Cxz

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find $f(x, y, z)$ such that $∇f(x, y, z) = F(x, y, z)$, where $F(x, y, z) = 2xyi + (x^{2} + 2z)j + 2yk$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z & =-x\operatorname{sin}⁡z+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡z+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xz+\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2xz+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+C.
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+(3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z})\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2xy{z}^{3} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) & =3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{y}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =-{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =-y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=-y{z}^{2}+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-2yz & =-2yz+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}-2z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x+y{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}+xy{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{e}^{z}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int \,\text{d}y \\  & =y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy{e}^{z}+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}-2z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{e}^{z}-2z & =xy{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2z \\ h(z) & =-{z}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{e}^{z}+{x}^{2}+y-{z}^{2}+C.
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,i+2yz\,j+{y}^{2}\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2yz\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (2yz)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{y}^{2}z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) & ={y}^{2} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{y}^{2}z+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (y+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =xy+x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x+z+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =z+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (z+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =yz+y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=yz+y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+x+yz+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =1 \\ h(z) & =z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+x+y+z+C.
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{z}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{z}^{2}+z \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int z\,\text{d}y \\  & =yz+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=yz+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+yz+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz+y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz+y-2$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz+y-2 & =2xyz+y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2 \\ h(z) & =-2z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+yz-2z+C.
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=(yz{e}^{xz}+z)\,i+({e}^{xz}+1)\,j+(xy{e}^{xz}+x)\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz{e}^{xz}+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (yz{e}^{xz}+z)\,\text{d}x \\  & =y{e}^{xz}+xz+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{xz}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{xz}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & ={e}^{xz}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 1\,\text{d}y \\  & =y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xz}+xz+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{xz}+x$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{e}^{xz}+x+{h}^{′}(z) & =zy{e}^{xz}+x \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=y{e}^{xz}+xz+y+C.
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=2x{y}^{3}z\,i+(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2})\,j+({x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz)\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{3}z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2x{y}^{3}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int {z}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y{z}^{2}+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+y{z}^{2}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz+{h}^{′}(z) & ={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+y{z}^{2}+C.
$$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y-2z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x+y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}+xy+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+x+z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2y+x+z \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2y+z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (2y+z)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}+yz+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}+yz+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy+{y}^{2}+yz+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y-2z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2z & =y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2z \\ h(z) & =-{z}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy+{y}^{2}+yz-{z}^{2}+C.
$$
